title: Daily decrease
hook: learning adds every day; the Tao subtracts every day (Tao Te Ching 48)

segments.voice: Yesterday, without going out the door: chapter forty-seven says one can understand the world without leaving home. Your line was at home. What did you notice, right where you live? Day one thousand one hundred ten.

How does a sculptor make an elephant out of a block of stone? The old joke answer: cut away everything that doesn't look like an elephant. It gets a laugh because it turns making things backward. Usually we add. We stack, collect, sign up, learn one more thing. Chapter forty-eight of the Tao Te Ching sets those two motions side by side, adding and taking away, and gives each one to a different kind of person.
screen: `AN ELEPHANT FROM A BLOCK OF STONE.` → `CUT AWAY WHAT ISN'T ELEPHANT.` → `ADDING, AND TAKING AWAY.`

segments.voice: First, the two paths. In James Legge's translation: "He who devotes himself to learning (seeks) from day to day to increase (his knowledge); he who devotes himself to the Tao (seeks) from day to day to diminish (his doing)." Learning adds. The way subtracts. Second, notice what the chapter doesn't say. It doesn't say learning is bad. It describes two different motions with two different aims. Learning fills the shelves. The way clears the floor. Legge's bracket says what gets cleared: doing. The busy pushing, the extra effort, the noise of trying too hard. Third, where the subtracting leads. The chapter says you lessen and lessen again, until you arrive at not forcing anything. Then it echoes chapter thirty-seven, from earlier: when nothing is forced, nothing is left undone. Chapter forty-eight adds that the world is won by not meddling, and lost by too much busyness. Fourth, the list. To-do lists tend to grow. A daily decrease turns the list over. What could come off today? One app you open without thinking. One commitment you said yes to out of guilt. One habit of explaining yourself over and over. One object that only collects dust. The way, in this chapter, isn't reached by adding a new practice on top of everything else. It's reached by setting something down, and then, tomorrow, setting down one more.
screen: `LEARNING ADDS, THE WAY SUBTRACTS.` · `CLEARING THE FLOOR, NOT THE SHELVES.` · `LESSEN, AND LESSEN AGAIN.` · `ONE THING OFF TODAY'S LIST.` · then, large: `DAILY DECREASE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remove one thing today. Settle and breathe out a little longer than you breathe in. With each long out-breath, let one thing go: the tension in your jaw, the grip in your hands, the plan you were rehearsing. Lessen, and lessen again. Then, near the end, let one thing from your actual day come to mind that could simply be dropped. Don't decide anything yet. Just notice how it feels to set it down. The bell holds the time.
Daily decrease. Chapter forty-eight: learning adds every day, and the way subtracts every day, until nothing is forced. Today's word.
Your line: less each day. Take one thing off today, an app, a task, an object, a habit, and see what the space feels like by tonight. Day one thousand one hundred ten.

howItsDone: Readers of the Tao Te Ching often take chapter forty-eight as a call to simplify, letting go of one habit, possession or effort at a time rather than adding new ones.

myth: chapter forty-eight says learning is bad
it describes two motions with two aims: learning adds, the way subtracts.
in Legge's bracket, what the way diminishes is doing
the extra effort and pushing, not knowledge itself.
the chapter says the world is won by being as busy as possible
it says the world is won by not meddling.

fork.setup: you want to grow on the way, and your week is already full. what does chapter forty-eight suggest?
options: add a new practice on top of everything.
take one thing away, then another.
learn more about the way first.
fork.reveal: the chapter says the one devoted to the way diminishes from day to day, lessening and lessening again.

original.note: Chinese: to decrease, to lessen; in chapter forty-eight, what the way does day by day.

trapdoor: what you thought: daily decrease means doing less work.
what it means: the way is reached by setting things down, one at a time, until nothing is forced.
what a scholar hears: Legge's brackets, increase (his knowledge) and diminish (his doing), and the chapter's link back to non-action.
